questions.q: The first table row defines chronotropy as ____ and assigns its regulation to ____.
opts: Heart rate; SA node / pacemaker potential
Conduction velocity; SA node / ventricular potential
questions.exp: Chronotropy means heart rate; its regulator is the SA node through pacemaker potential. (Book p387)

questions.q: Which meaning and regulator belong to the inotropy row?
opts: Myocardial contractility; ventricle (left > right), ventricular potential
Myocardial relaxation; ventricle (right > left), ventricular potential
Myocardial contractility; atria (left > right), pacemaker potential
Heart rate; SA node, pacemaker potential
questions.exp: Inotropy is myocardial contractility, regulated by the ventricle (Lt > Rt) and ventricular potential. (Book p387)

questions.q: Match the remaining rows; all three regulator cells are printed as dashes — 1) Dromotropy 2) Bathmotropy 3) Lusitropy … A) Cardiac conduction velocity B) Cardiac excitability C) Cardiac relaxation
questions.exp: Dromotropy is conduction velocity, bathmotropy excitability and lusitropy relaxation. Their regulator cells are all dashes; no regulator is supplied. (Book p387)

questions.q: Using only this page’s printed heart-failure split, which pair is correct?
questions.exp: The printed flowchart uses <50% and >50%, leaving exactly 50% unspecified. These are book-specific cutoffs, not the full contemporary EF classification. (Book p387)

questions.q: In the older-classification table, impaired contractility and impaired relaxation map respectively to which dysfunctions?
questions.exp: The older table pairs systolic dysfunction with impaired contractility and diastolic dysfunction with impaired relaxation. (Book p387)

questions.q: True or false: the older table says diastolic dysfunction always requires accompanying systolic dysfunction.
opts: True — impaired relaxation is another name for impaired contractility
False — diastolic may occur with or without systolic dysfunction; systolic is listed as always accompanied by diastolic
True — the table gives an obligatory systolic component for diastolic dysfunction
False — neither type can ever coexist with the other
questions.exp: The systolic column says always associated with diastolic dysfunction; the diastolic column says ± systolic dysfunction. (Book p387)

questions.q: Which treatment-row wording belongs to the book’s explicitly older classification (not current prescribing advice)?
opts: Systolic: treatment options present; diastolic: “No drugs to Rx”
Systolic: no drugs; diastolic: treatment options present
Both columns: no drugs to treat
questions.exp: The older table prints Rx options + under systolic and No drugs to Rx under diastolic. The latter is a historical/source statement and must not be used as contemporary HFpEF treatment advice. (Book p387)

questions.q: Automaticity means the heart can beat ____.
opts: Only when AV conduction is intact
questions.exp: The book defines automaticity as the ability of the heart to beat in the absence of stimuli. (Book p387)

questions.q: Which listed site is singled out as the pacemaker with maximum potential?
questions.exp: The SA node is specifically marked pacemaker (maximum potential). (Book p387)

questions.q: Which replacement would make the printed automaticity-site list incorrect?
opts: Dense fibrous tissue instead of atrial cells
Distal AV node alongside the SA node
Ventricular myocardium alongside the His–Purkinje system
questions.exp: The listed sites are SA node, distal AV node, atrial cells, His–Purkinje system and ventricular myocardium—not dense fibrous tissue. (Book p387)

questions.q: For the pacemaker-potential phase, the book pairs transient outward K channels with ____ and inward rectifying K channels with ____.
questions.exp: The printed sequence is TOK: transient outward K, closure; IRK: inward rectifying K, opening. This item tests the source’s channel wording rather than silently rewriting it. (Book p387)

questions.q: The funny-current channel is expanded as ____ and is listed as opening during pacemaker potential.
questions.exp: The line names hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide (HCN) channel and labels funny currents (opening). (Book p387)

questions.q: Which combination matches all three continuation bullets for HCN/funny-current channels?
opts: Na channels; rods, cones and olfactory epithelium; digoxin
Ca channels; rods, cones and atrial septum; ivabradine
Na channels; rods, cones and olfactory epithelium; ivabradine
K channels; rods, cones and olfactory epithelium; a beta-blocker
questions.exp: The book lists Na channels, sites in rods/cones/olfactory epithelium, and blockade by ivabradine. HCN current is physiologically a mixed-cation current; “Na channels” is the source’s shorthand. (Book p388)

questions.q: Match each phase to the printed channel event — 1) Late pacemaker-potential sequence 2) Depolarisation 3) Repolarisation … A) L-type calcium channel activity B) L-type calcium closure plus delayed rectifier K opening C) T-type calcium channel opening
questions.exp: T-type calcium opening completes the pacemaker-potential list. Depolarisation uses L-type calcium; repolarisation closes L-type calcium and opens DRK, delayed rectifier K channels. (Book p388)

questions.q: On the pacemaker-potential graph, which reading correctly follows the labelled slope, upstroke and downstroke?
opts: The pacemaker slope is flat; Na efflux drives the upstroke; K influx drives the downstroke
Membrane potential falls toward threshold; K influx drives the upstroke; Ca efflux drives the downstroke
Membrane potential rises toward threshold; Ca influx drives the upstroke; K efflux with reduced Ca permeability accompanies the downstroke
The slope starts only after the upstroke; Ca permeability falls on the upstroke and rises on the downstroke
questions.exp: The axes are membrane potential (mV) against time (s). The labelled pacemaker slope approaches threshold; the upstroke is marked increased Ca permeability/influx, and repolarisation increased K with decreased Ca permeability and K efflux. (Book p388)

questions.q: Match the four numbered markers on the pacemaker-potential curve — 1) Marker 1 2) Marker 2 3) Marker 3 4) Marker 4 … A) Falling repolarisation limb B) Rapid rising limb C) Transition from slow slope to threshold/upstroke D) Near the most negative potential
questions.exp: Markers 1–4 sit near the negative trough, the threshold transition, the rising limb and the falling limb respectively. They are diagram call-out numbers, not ventricular action-potential phase numbers. (Book p388)

questions.q: Which pair reproduces the scale/time call-outs on the pacemaker-potential illustration?
opts: Voltage scale −90 to +40 mV; time annotation 800 msec
Voltage scale −90 to +40 mV; time annotation 80 msec
Voltage scale −60 to +20 mV; time annotation 80 msec
Voltage scale −60 to +20 mV; time annotation 800 msec
questions.exp: The figure’s membrane-potential scale runs from −60 to +20 mV and its time annotation reads 800 msec; these are figure labels, not universal cycle durations. (Book p388)

questions.q: In the bradyarrhythmia impulse-pathway figure, the sequence after sinus node and atria is ____.
opts: Bundle of His → AV node → bundle branches → ventricles
AV node → bundle of His → bundle branches → ventricles
AV node → bundle branches → bundle of His → ventricles
Bundle branches → bundle of His → AV node → ventricles
questions.exp: The figure shows sinus node in the atria, then AV node, His bundle, bundle branches and ventricles. (Book p388)

questions.q: Which description correctly identifies the diagram’s bracket and separating tissue?
opts: His and sinus node form the bracketed AV system; Purkinje fibres form the separating sheet
AV node, His and bundle branches form the bracketed AV system; dense fibrous tissue separates atria and ventricles
Only the ventricles form the bracketed AV system; atrial muscle is labelled dense fibrous tissue
Sinus node and atria form the bracketed AV system; ventricular muscle separates the chambers
questions.exp: The bracket encloses AV node, bundle of His and bundle branches; dense fibrous tissue is labelled at the atrioventricular boundary. (Book p388)

questions.q: Which is NOT one of the four level categories listed under heart blocks?
opts: AV block of first, second or third degree
questions.exp: The listed levels/categories are SA node, sinoatrial block, AV block (1°, 2°, 3°), and fascicular block. (Book p388)

questions.q: Match each arm of the fascicular-block flowchart — 1) Unifascicular 2) Bifascicular 3) Trifascicular … A) LAFB, LPFB or RBBB alone B) Bifascicular block plus increased PR interval C) RBBB plus LAFB/LPFB, or LBBB
questions.exp: These are the three arms exactly as classified on this page. Prolonged PR alone does not establish the anatomical site of additional conduction delay. (Book p388)

questions.q: The sinus-node-dysfunction strip A illustrates loss of ____ after the last displayed beat.
opts: Only S waves with preserved sinus P waves
Only T waves with preserved sinus P waves
Only the PR segment with continuing normal beats
questions.exp: The heading states absent P waves; strip A shows a preceding beat followed by a flat continuation, captioned sinus node dysfunction. (Book p388)

questions.q: After sinus failure, a regular escape rhythm is 50 bpm with no P waves. Which comparison matches the compensation line?
opts: Atrial escape has no P; junctional escape has abnormal P; both are 40–60 bpm
Junctional escape has no P; atrial escape has abnormal P; both are listed at 40–60 bpm
Both escape types require normal P waves and rates of 15–40 bpm
Junctional escape has normal P; atrial escape has absent P; both are 60–100 bpm
questions.exp: The line gives junctional rhythm (no P wave) or atrial rhythm (abnormal P wave), 40–60 bpm; the illustrated strip is junctional escape rhythm. (Book p388)

questions.q: The first extrinsic cause in the sinus-dysfunction flowchart is ____.
questions.exp: The causes branch into extrinsic and intrinsic; hyperkalemia heads the extrinsic list. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which drug is NOT in this page’s three-item extrinsic drug list?
questions.exp: The printed drug list is digoxin, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers. Ivabradine appears in the earlier HCN discussion, not this particular list; this is not a claim that it cannot cause bradycardia. (Book p389)

questions.q: The increased-PaCO2 (hypercapnia) bullet names ____ as its associated syndrome.
questions.exp: The extrinsic-cause list links increased PaCO2/hypercapnia to obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome. (Book p389)

questions.q: Match the remaining extrinsic-cause lines — 1) Low body temperature 2) Myxedema coma 3) Increased intracranial tension … A) Bradycardia–hypertension reflex B) Hypothyroidism C) Hypothermia
questions.exp: The remaining bullets are hypothermia, hypothyroidism (myxedema coma), and increased intracranial tension with the bradycardia–hypertension reflex. (Book p389)

questions.q: After the extrinsic list, which diagnosis occupies the intrinsic arm?
questions.exp: The intrinsic arm contains sick sinus syndrome, in contrast to the preceding extrinsic metabolic, drug and systemic causes. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which combination is explicitly marked on the upper-right SA-nodal-dysfunction tracing?
questions.exp: The figure annotations identify hyperkalemia in the tall-wave area and junctional rhythm in the circled rhythm-strip complexes. (Book p389)

questions.q: A regular 48-bpm tracing has normal P waves before its complexes. Which source-based interpretation and cause weighting fit?
opts: Atrial escape; equal weighting of extrinsic and intrinsic causes
Sinus bradycardia; extrinsic causes far outweigh intrinsic causes
Junctional escape; intrinsic causes far outweigh extrinsic causes
Sinus bradycardia; intrinsic causes far outweigh extrinsic causes
questions.exp: The sinus-bradycardia bullets specify regular rhythm, 40–60 bpm, normal P waves and extrinsic >> intrinsic causes; the adjacent strip illustrates this pattern. (Book p389)

questions.q: In the two labelled pause diagrams, sinus pause/arrest has ____ and sinoatrial exit block has ____.
opts: Distance A = B; distance A > B
Distance A < B; distance A = B
Distance A = B; distance A < B
Distance A > B; distance A = B
questions.exp: The captions under the diagrams explicitly read distance A > B for sinus pause/arrest and distance A = B for sinoatrial exit block. These refer to the labelled diagram spans. (Book p389)

questions.q: The third manifestation’s strip alternates rapid activity with a slow phase. Which caption belongs to it?
questions.exp: The third ECG manifestation is captioned tachy-brady syndrome. (Book p389)

questions.q: The idioventricular-rhythm heading explicitly associates IVR with a ____ QRS complex.
questions.exp: IVR is followed by an arrow to wide QRS complex. (Book p389)

questions.q: Which pair matches the first two printed ventricular-rate categories?
opts: IVR up to 40 bpm; AIVR 40–100 bpm
IVR up to 60 bpm; AIVR 60–100 bpm
IVR 40–100 bpm; AIVR up to 40 bpm
IVR up to 40 bpm; AIVR >100 bpm
questions.exp: The bullets give IVR up to 40 and accelerated IVR 40–100 bpm. Exactly 40 overlaps in the printed wording and is not a reliable discriminator here. (Book p389)

questions.q: Following reperfusion, a wide-complex ventricular rhythm runs at 70 bpm. What does the AIVR sub-bullet suggest?
opts: Ordinary IVR — a marker of failed reperfusion
Junctional escape — because all escape rhythms are 40–100 bpm
Ventricular tachycardia — because any rate above 40 is VT
Accelerated IVR — a marker of successful reperfusion
questions.exp: The AIVR sub-bullet calls the rhythm a marker of successful reperfusion. (Book p389)

questions.q: The final rate bullet labels a ventricular rhythm at 110 bpm ____.
questions.exp: The book labels a ventricular rhythm with HR >100 bpm ventricular tachycardia. (Book p389)

questions.q: The adjacent wide-complex ECG with circled rhythm-strip complexes is captioned AIVR. Which expansion belongs to that caption?
questions.exp: AIVR expands to accelerated idioventricular rhythm, the caption beneath the marked ECG. (Book p389)

questions.q: True or false: the bottom AV-block strip B contrasts with sinus dysfunction by showing absent QRS complexes while atrial P waves continue.
opts: True — the AV-block bullet identifies absent QRS complexes
False — the missing components are only T waves
True — AV block is defined here by loss of all P waves as well
False — the AV-block caption refers to an isolated prolonged QT
questions.exp: The AV-block heading says absent QRS complexes; its strip continues P waves without the corresponding ventricular complexes. (Book p389)

units.title: Cardiac Terminology & Heart-Failure Tables
units.guide:
Connect each cardiac term to its function and the regulator named in the table.
Read the heart-failure cutoffs and older systolic/diastolic comparison as source-specific teaching, not a current treatment guideline.

units.title: Automaticity & Pacemaker Potential
units.guide:
Identify the tissues capable of automaticity and the SA node’s leading role.
Follow the printed channel sequence across the page break, separating pacemaker slope, depolarisation and repolarisation.

units.title: Heart Blocks & Escape Pathways
units.guide:
Trace the AV conduction-system figure, including the insulating fibrous tissue.
Classify each fascicular branch and distinguish absent sinus P waves from compensating atrial or junctional activity.

units.title: Sinus Dysfunction: Causes & ECG Manifestations
units.guide:
Separate intrinsic sick sinus syndrome from the complete extrinsic-cause list.
Then distinguish sinus bradycardia, pause/arrest, exit block and tachy-brady patterns.
Use QRS width and rate to classify ventricular escape and recognise the AV-block contrast.
